screens.title: Optimizing Game Code with Modern C++ Features
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll learn practical modern C++ tools that make game code both faster and safer. You will see how small annotations like const and the right constructors can allow the compiler to avoid work, and how move semantics let your engine transfer ownership of big buffers without expensive copying. We'll examine concrete code from texture and mesh classes, step through move constructors and move assignment operators, and compare when copies happen versus when moves are used. Finally, we'll tour smart pointers — unique ownership for single owners and shared ownership with reference counting — to prevent leaks and dangling pointers in systems like resource managers. These techniques directly affect frame time: fewer deep copies mean less C P U time and fewer cache churns when handling vertex buffers, textures, or large game state objects. A quick example: returning a large texture or mesh from a factory should move its internal buffer instead of copying it. That simple change saves milliseconds across many objects. As you explore, ask yourself which large structure in your project would most benefit from a move rather than a copy.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to write safer, faster C++ code for game systems. First, you will understand const correctness: how marking parameters and member functions as constant prevents accidental changes and allows compilers to assume immutability. Second, you will explain lvalue and rvalue references and why temporaries behave differently from named objects. Third, you will implement move constructors and move assignment operators so your classes can transfer internal buffers cheaply instead of copying them. Finally, you will use smart pointers to manage ownership: decide when exclusive ownership with a unique pointer is appropriate and when shared ownership with reference counting is necessary. Each objective ties to real game scenarios — textures, meshes, resource managers, and vectors used in rendering or physics — and you will practice writing and reading code that demonstrates the difference in behavior. These skills reduce frame spikes caused by unexpected deep copies, prevent common memory leaks, and make your intent explicit to other developers. A short practice activity will guide you through implementing moves for a Mesh and verifying that moves reduce costly allocations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills Breakdown
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives break down into concrete skills you can use in game systems today. You will learn to mark getters and query functions as constant so they can be called on immutable objects and so the compiler can help catch unintended changes. screens.title: Const Correctness
screens.narratorSegment: Const correctness is a small discipline that yields big benefits in game code. When you mark a member function as constant, you promise it will not change the object state. That promise helps other developers understand your intent and allows the compiler to assume immutability in optimizations. For example, a GetPosition method on a game object should be const because asking for a value must not modify the object. Passing large objects by const reference avoids expensive copies while protecting the original from modification. A key practical rule is: prefer const references for read-only parameters, and reserve pass-by-value only when you need to take ownership or perform a cheap move. A common misconception is thinking const is only about preventing reassignment; it is also a signal that the callee will not alter state, which reduces bugs in systems like rendering or physics where accidental changes propagate widely. Another pitfall is failing to mark methods const and then being unable to call them on constant objects or containers of const elements. Concrete example: if your ResourceManager hands out const Texture& to rendering code, you avoid copying large pixel buffers and guarantee they will not be modified. Takeaway: use const as a design tool to express intent, avoid accidental state changes, and enable safer optimizations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Const Correctness
Definition

Declare variables, parameters, and member functions as const when they should not change. This documents intent and allows optimizations.

Why it matters
Prevents accidental mutation, reduces bugs in systems that share references, and helps the compiler.
Common mistake
Not marking getters const so they cannot be used on const objects or in constexpr contexts.
Key Takeaway

Use const to express intent and avoid copies by passing large objects as const references when mutation is not required.

Example and explanation
class GameObject {
  Vector3 position;
public:
  Vector3 getPosition() const { return position; } // const method: no mutation
  void setPosition(const Vector3& p) { position = p; }
};

void render(const GameObject& obj) {
  auto pos = obj.getPosition(); // safe: no copy of object, only returned value
}
Practical mnemonic
Think: const = promise. If you promise not to change, callers can rely on stability.
Check
If a function is a pure query, mark it const. If it needs ownership, accept by value or move.

screens.title: Applying const in APIs and Member Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Designing APIs with const in mind means thinking like a caller first. Start by asking which functions should be allowed to mutate an object's internal state and which should only observe it. For observer functions, mark them const. For parameters, prefer const references for large objects you do not need to modify, for example const Texture& or const Mesh&. If the callee needs to take ownership, prefer pass-by-value combined with move, or accept an rvalue reference for explicit transfers. A typical pattern in game code is factory functions that return heavy objects by value and rely on move constructors to transfer buffers without copies. Another useful pattern is separating const and non-const overloads: provide both const T& and T& accessors as needed so callers with const objects can still read data. A common misuse is returning a non-const reference to internal buffers, which leaks implementation details and allows accidental modification. Concrete example: a ResourceManager might offer const references to loaded textures for renderers, but offer unique_ptr factories for systems that want ownership and lifecycle control. This design reduces accidental mutations and keeps allocation behavior predictable. As you design APIs, document ownership clearly and choose signatures that express intent — const for read-only, unique ownership for single owners, and shared pointers when multiple owners must extend lifetime.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Const APIs
Step-by-step: choose the right signature
Step 1: Read or mutate?
If the function only observes, make it const or take a const reference.
Step 2: Ownership needed?
If the function must keep the object, accept by value and move, or accept a unique pointer to clarify transfer.
Step 3: Shared lifetime?
Use shared pointers only when multiple systems must keep the resource alive.
Key Takeaway

Match function signatures to ownership and mutation intent to make code safe and efficient.

Examples
// Read-only: no copy of heavy object
void render(const Texture& t);

// Take ownership: caller can move
void addToCache(Texture t);

// Explicit transfer of ownership
void setActive(std::unique_ptr texture);
Misconception
Passing by value always copies. Not if you move into the parameter or the caller moves before call.
Pro tip
Document ownership in function comments: this avoids confusion in large engine codebases.

screens.title: Lvalues and Rvalues
screens.narratorSegment: Lvalues and rvalues are foundational to move semantics. An lvalue is an expression that refers to an identifiable object with a stable address — a named variable you can take the address of. An rvalue is a temporary value that does not persist beyond the expression, like a literal or the return value of a function. The distinction matters because rvalues are safe to steal resources from: the object will be destroyed soon anyway. Rvalue references, declared with double ampersand, bind to rvalues and allow code to implement move semantics by taking ownership of internal buffers. A common pitfall is treating a named variable as an rvalue without explicitly converting it, which can lead to unexpected moves or copies. For example, when you want to move a named object into another, you must explicitly cast using the standard move operation to indicate transfer intent. Concrete example: returning a large vector from a factory function produces an rvalue that the receiving variable can use via move construction, avoiding a deep copy of internal buffers. Misconception to watch for: not every temporary is cheap; moving still requires leaving the source in a valid state, so implement move operations correctly. The skill is to recognize when an expression is a temporary and when you must request a move explicitly for a named object.

keyIdea.text: Lvalue = named, addressable object. Rvalue = temporary. Use rvalue references to implement efficient transfers from temporaries.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Lvalue vs Rvalue
Definitions
  • Lvalue: an object with identity and address, like a named variable.
  • Rvalue: a temporary value that will be discarded, like a function return.
  • Rvalue reference (&&): binds to temporaries and allows stealing resources.
Misconception
You do not implicitly move from named variables; you must indicate move intent explicitly to avoid surprising state changes.
Concrete example
// Function returns an rvalue (temporary)
std::vector makeBuffer() { return std::vector(100000); }

// Receiving a temporary uses move construction when available
std::vector buf = makeBuffer(); // no deep copy if move is available

// Named variable must be explicitly moved
std::vector a = buf; // copy
std::vector b = std::move(buf); // move: ownership transferred
Pro tip
Recognize temporaries in expressions to let your types benefit from automatic moves.

screens.title: Move Semantics
screens.narratorSegment: Move semantics allow your classes to transfer ownership of internal resources—pointers, buffers, handles—without making costly deep copies. The key idea is to implement a move constructor and move assignment operator that take an rvalue reference and steal the internal pointer, then leave the source in a valid but empty state. When you write a move constructor, you copy the pointer values and reset the source pointer to null. This pattern saves time and memory bandwidth when creating or returning large objects, such as textures, meshes, or particle buffers. A common mistake is forgetting to reset the moved-from object, which can result in double deletes or dangling pointers. Another pitfall is failing to declare move operations noexcept; many standard containers will only move elements during reallocation if moves are noexcept, otherwise they fall back to copying. Concrete example: a Texture class that allocates pixel data can implement a move constructor that transfers the data pointer and sets the original pointer to null. When such objects are returned from factories or inserted into vectors, moves eliminate deep copy loops. Takeaway: implement correct, noexcept move operations and ensure moved-from objects remain destructible and safe to ignore.

keyIdea.title: Move pattern
keyIdea.text: Implement move constructor to transfer raw pointers and reset the source; declare noexcept when possible to enable optimizations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Move Semantics
What to implement
  • Move constructor: take rvalue, steal pointers, reset source.
  • Move assignment: release own resources, steal, reset source, return *this.
  • Prefer noexcept to enable moves in containers.
Misconception
Moving is free. It is cheap relative to copying but still requires pointer swaps and state updates.
Checklist
Leave moved-from valid and destructible.
Declare noexcept where safe to help standard containers prefer move.
Avoid duplicating code by reusing move logic in assignment.
Key Takeaway

Move operations let you transfer ownership cheaply; implement them correctly and mark noexcept to get the most benefit.

The class allocates a dynamic array for pixel data in the constructor, performs a deep copy in the copy constructor and copy assignment, and implements move operations that steal the pointer and reset the source. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Texture Example
Texture class (excerpt)
class Texture {
private:
    unsigned int* textureData;
    int width, height;
public:
    Texture() : textureData(nullptr), width(0), height(0) {}

    Texture(int w, int h) : width(w), height(h) {
        textureData = new unsigned int[width * height];
        // simulate load
        std::cout << "Texture created: " << width << "x" << height << std::endl;
    }

    // Copy constructor (deep)
    Texture(const Texture& other) : width(other.width), height(other.height) {
        if (other.textureData) {
            textureData = new unsigned int[width * height];
            std::copy(other.textureData, other.textureData + (width * height), textureData);
        } else textureData = nullptr;
        std::cout << "Texture copied." << std::endl;
    }

    // Move constructor (steals resources)
    Texture(Texture&& other) noexcept : textureData(other.textureData), width(other.width), height(other.height) {
        other.textureData = nullptr; other.width = 0; other.height = 0;
        std::cout << "Texture moved (constructor)." << std::endl;
    }

    ~Texture() { if (textureData) delete[] textureData; }
};

Texture createBigTexture() { return Texture(1024, 768); }

int main() {
    Texture t1(512,512);
    Texture t2 = t1;              // copy
    Texture t3 = createBigTexture(); // move
}
Explanation
  • Copy constructor performs allocation and element-wise copy — expensive for large textures.
  • Move constructor reuses the data pointer and leaves the source empty — fast and allocation-free.
  • Declaring move operations noexcept helps containers prefer moves during reallocation.
Check
Run the program and observe the printed messages to confirm whether copies or moves occurred.

screens.title: Move Constructor and Assignment — Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing move constructor and move assignment, follow a clear sequence. For a move constructor: take the source's pointers and counters, set the source pointers to null and its counters to zero, and ensure noexcept if the operation cannot fail. For move assignment: guard self-assignment, release your current resources, steal the source resources, reset the source, and return *this. A concrete pitfall is forgetting to delete existing resources before stealing, causing a leak, or deleting after stealing, causing a double free. Another is leaving the source in an inconsistent state; always leave it destructible and safe to ignore. Many standard containers check for noexcept move constructors before choosing move over copy during reallocation, so marking your move operations noexcept can improve performance indirectly. Use runtime prints during development to confirm which path (copy or move) is taken in your code paths. Example usage shows a call to a factory that returns a texture; the move constructor should be invoked and the large allocation avoided. After implementing, test by returning large objects from functions and by pushing objects into vectors to ensure moves, not copies, are being used.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Move Implementation
Move assignment pattern
Texture& Texture::operator=(Texture&& other) noexcept {
  if (this != &other) {
    delete[] textureData; // release current resource
    textureData = other.textureData;
    width = other.width; height = other.height;
    other.textureData = nullptr; other.width = 0; other.height = 0;
  }
  std::cout << "Texture moved (assignment)." << std::endl;
  return *this;
}
Pitfalls
Always delete existing resources before stealing. Mark noexcept so containers will prefer moves when resizing.
Verification
  1. Run tests where functions return large objects; observe move messages.
  2. Push many objects into a vector to see whether moves happen during reallocation.
  3. Check for leaks or double deletes with tools or by careful destructor logging.
Key Takeaway

Test moves with runtime logs and prefer noexcept moves so standard containers use them during reallocation.

screens.title: Copy vs Move — Performance Comparison
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing copy and move operations in the context of game objects makes the difference concrete. A deep copy duplicates internal buffers and triggers heap allocations proportional to the buffer size, incurring C P U time and memory bandwidth. Moving transfers pointer ownership and adjusts a few integers; there is no allocation and often minimal branch cost. Consider returning a large vertex buffer from a mesh factory in a tight loop. With copies, each return causes a deep allocation and element-wise copy that can dominate C P U time. With moves, the temporary's pointer is transferred; only a small constant-time pointer swap occurs. Another important effect is cache behavior: copying large buffers increases cache pressure and can evict frequently used data, while moving avoids that churn. However, moves still require careful design: moved-from objects should be safe to destroy, and you should ensure no dangling references remain. A common misconception is that using smart pointers removes the need for moves; smart pointers manage lifetime, but moving the smart pointer itself still transfers ownership cheaply. In short, prefer move semantics for large, heap-backed resources and measure the difference with profiler traces or allocation counters to guide optimization efforts.

With moves, the temporary's pointer is transferred; only a small constant-time pointer swap occurs. However, moves still require careful design: moved-from objects should be safe to destroy, and you should ensure no dangling references remain. screens.title: Smart Pointers: std::unique_ptr
screens.narratorSegment: std::unique_ptr is the simplest smart pointer: it represents exclusive ownership of a dynamically allocated object and automatically deletes it when the unique pointer goes out of scope. Use unique pointer for resources that have one clear owner, such as a component attached to a single entity or a temporary resource loaded for a single task. A unique pointer has minimal runtime overhead and often compiles down to the same cost as a raw pointer plus a destructor call. It also communicates intent: when you see unique pointer in a signature, you know the caller or callee controls lifetime. Transfer of ownership is explicit and cheap via move semantics; copying is disabled for unique pointers which prevents accidental duplicates. Concrete example: a factory function can return a unique pointer to a game object using a make-unique helper so the caller becomes the new owner. A common misconception is thinking unique pointer forbids moving — it does allow moving, which is the intended way to transfer ownership. When designing systems, prefer unique pointer unless multiple owners are required, and use it to eliminate manual delete calls and reduce leak risk.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › std::unique_ptr
Example
std::unique_ptr createEnemy(const std::string& name) {
    return std::make_unique(name);
}

int main() {
    auto player = std::make_unique("Player");
    auto boss = createEnemy("Dragon"); // ownership transferred to caller
}
Why use it
Eliminates manual delete, expresses single ownership, and transfers ownership via move only.
Notes
  • Copying unique pointer is not allowed — only moving expresses transfer.

  • Unique pointer is ideal for component ownership in an entity-component system.

screens.title: std::shared_ptr and Lifetime Management
screens.narratorSegment: std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership using reference counting. Several systems can hold a shared pointer to the same object; the object is destroyed only when the last shared pointer is destroyed. This is useful for resources that multiple entities reference, such as a texture atlas or a sound asset referenced by many game objects. The trade-off is slight overhead for maintaining the reference count and the potential for memory leaks caused by cyclic references. To avoid cycles, use a weak pointer to hold a non-owning reference that can be checked for validity. Concrete example: a ResourceManager returns a shared pointer to a texture; many entities store that pointer and the texture is freed automatically when all references are gone. You can observe the reference count using the use_count method during debugging. Misconception: shared pointers eliminate all lifetime problems — they only manage ownership but cannot fix circular dependencies without weak pointers. Use shared pointers when multiple independent owners need to keep a resource alive and use weak pointers for observer references to break cycles. When performance matters, measure the overhead; sometimes storing raw handles with explicit management is acceptable, but shared pointers are a safer default in many engine subsystems.

Example
auto tex = std::make_shared("SharedTexture");
std::vector> entities;
entities.push_back(tex);
entities.push_back(std::make_shared("ParticleSystem"));

screens.title: Activity: Implement Move Semantics for Mesh
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement the move constructor and move assignment operator for a Mesh class that manages a dynamic Vertex array. The starter code allocates vertices in the constructor, implements deep copy in copy operations, and provides a destructor. Your tasks are: implement a move constructor that steals the vertex pointer and the vertex count, then reset the source to a safe empty state; implement move assignment that releases current resources, steals from the source, and resets it; and mark both move operations noexcept if safe. After implementing, test by returning Mesh objects from a factory and by moving named Mesh instances with the standard move operation. Verify results by printing messages in constructors and by checking vertex counts after moves to ensure the source shows zero. A key verification is to push many Mesh instances into a vector and observe construction messages — with noexcept moves, the vector will prefer moves on reallocation. Avoid deleting a pointer that you stole from the source or leaving the moved-from object with dangling pointers. This exercise demonstrates how moving large vertex arrays avoids repeated heap allocations and reduces per-frame overhead.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Mesh Move Activity
Starter code (excerpt)
struct Vertex { float x,y,z; };

class Mesh {
private:
  Vertex* vertices;
  size_t vertexCount;
public:
  Mesh() : vertices(nullptr), vertexCount(0) {}
  Mesh(size_t count) : vertexCount(count) { vertices = new Vertex[vertexCount]; }
  ~Mesh() { if (vertices) delete[] vertices; }

  Mesh(const Mesh& other) : vertexCount(other.vertexCount) {
    if (other.vertices) {
      vertices = new Vertex[vertexCount];
      std::copy(other.vertices, other.vertices + vertexCount, vertices);
    } else vertices = nullptr;
  }

  Mesh& operator=(const Mesh& other) { /* copy assignment provided */ }

  // TODO: Implement move constructor
  // TODO: Implement move assignment operator

  size_t getVertexCount() const { return vertexCount; }
};
Verification steps
  1. Implement move operations and mark noexcept when safe.
  2. Create and return Mesh from a factory and confirm move constructor used.
  3. Move a named Mesh with std::move and ensure counts transfer and source is zero.
Hints and pitfalls
  • In move assignment, free your existing memory before stealing the source pointer to avoid leaks.
  • Reset the moved-from vertex pointer to nullptr and vertexCount to zero so destructor is safe.
  • Mark moves noexcept when you don't throw to encourage container moves.

Implement moves, test with factories and vectors, and confirm the moved-from object is safe to destroy and shows zero vertices.

In this lesson we'll learn practical modern C++ tools that make game code both faster and safer. You will see how small annotations like const and the right constructors can allow the compiler to avoid work, and how move semantics let your engine transfer ownership of big buffers without expensive copying. We'll examine concrete code from texture and mesh classes, step through move constructors and move assignment operators, and compare when copies happen versus when moves are used. Finally, we'll tour smart pointers — unique ownership for single owners and shared ownership with reference counting — to prevent leaks and dangling pointers in systems like resource managers. These techniques directly affect frame time: fewer deep copies mean less C P U time and fewer cache churns when handling vertex buffers, textures, or large game state objects. A quick example: returning a large texture or mesh from a factory should move its internal buffer instead of copying it. That simple change saves milliseconds across many objects. As you explore, ask yourself which large structure in your project would most benefit from a move rather than a copy.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write safer, faster C++ code for game systems. First, you will understand const correctness: how marking parameters and member functions as constant prevents accidental changes and allows compilers to assume immutability. Second, you will explain lvalue and rvalue references and why temporaries behave differently from named objects. Third, you will implement move constructors and move assignment operators so your classes can transfer internal buffers cheaply instead of copying them. Finally, you will use smart pointers to manage ownership: decide when exclusive ownership with a unique pointer is appropriate and when shared ownership with reference counting is necessary. Each objective ties to real game scenarios — textures, meshes, resource managers, and vectors used in rendering or physics — and you will practice writing and reading code that demonstrates the difference in behavior. These skills reduce frame spikes caused by unexpected deep copies, prevent common memory leaks, and make your intent explicit to other developers. A short practice activity will guide you through implementing moves for a Mesh and verifying that moves reduce costly allocations.

These objectives break down into concrete skills you can use in game systems today. You will learn to mark getters and query functions as constant so they can be called on immutable objects and so the compiler can help catch unintended changes. You will practice identifying lvalues and rvalues in expressions, which helps when you decide whether to use pass-by-value, pass-by-const-reference, or an rvalue reference to accept ownership. You will implement move constructors and move assignments that leave the moved-from object in a valid but empty state, avoiding double deletes. Finally, you'll choose between unique pointers for single owner components such as a mesh attached to one entity, or shared pointers for resources accessed by many entities and stored in resource caches. Each skill reduces runtime overhead: fewer deep copies reduce allocations and improve cache coherence, while smart pointers reduce leaks and unpredictable lifetime issues. After practicing, you should be able to read a class and immediately tell whether it will copy heavy data or move it, and adjust the A P I accordingly.

Const correctness is a small discipline that yields big benefits in game code. When you mark a member function as constant, you promise it will not change the object state. That promise helps other developers understand your intent and allows the compiler to assume immutability in optimizations. For example, a GetPosition method on a game object should be const because asking for a value must not modify the object. Passing large objects by const reference avoids expensive copies while protecting the original from modification. A key practical rule is: prefer const references for read-only parameters, and reserve pass-by-value only when you need to take ownership or perform a cheap move. A common misconception is thinking const is only about preventing reassignment; it is also a signal that the callee will not alter state, which reduces bugs in systems like rendering or physics where accidental changes propagate widely. Another pitfall is failing to mark methods const and then being unable to call them on constant objects or containers of const elements. Concrete example: if your ResourceManager hands out const Texture& to rendering code, you avoid copying large pixel buffers and guarantee they will not be modified. Takeaway: use const as a design tool to express intent, avoid accidental state changes, and enable safer optimizations.

Designing APIs with const in mind means thinking like a caller first. Start by asking which functions should be allowed to mutate an object's internal state and which should only observe it. For observer functions, mark them const. For parameters, prefer const references for large objects you do not need to modify, for example const Texture& or const Mesh&. If the callee needs to take ownership, prefer pass-by-value combined with move, or accept an rvalue reference for explicit transfers. A typical pattern in game code is factory functions that return heavy objects by value and rely on move constructors to transfer buffers without copies. Another useful pattern is separating const and non-const overloads: provide both const T& and T& accessors as needed so callers with const objects can still read data. A common misuse is returning a non-const reference to internal buffers, which leaks implementation details and allows accidental modification. Concrete example: a ResourceManager might offer const references to loaded textures for renderers, but offer unique_ptr factories for systems that want ownership and lifecycle control. This design reduces accidental mutations and keeps allocation behavior predictable. As you design APIs, document ownership clearly and choose signatures that express intent — const for read-only, unique ownership for single owners, and shared pointers when multiple owners must extend lifetime.

Lvalues and rvalues are foundational to move semantics. An lvalue is an expression that refers to an identifiable object with a stable address — a named variable you can take the address of. An rvalue is a temporary value that does not persist beyond the expression, like a literal or the return value of a function. The distinction matters because rvalues are safe to steal resources from: the object will be destroyed soon anyway. Rvalue references, declared with double ampersand, bind to rvalues and allow code to implement move semantics by taking ownership of internal buffers. A common pitfall is treating a named variable as an rvalue without explicitly converting it, which can lead to unexpected moves or copies. For example, when you want to move a named object into another, you must explicitly cast using the standard move operation to indicate transfer intent. Concrete example: returning a large vector from a factory function produces an rvalue that the receiving variable can use via move construction, avoiding a deep copy of internal buffers. Misconception to watch for: not every temporary is cheap; moving still requires leaving the source in a valid state, so implement move operations correctly. The skill is to recognize when an expression is a temporary and when you must request a move explicitly for a named object.

Move semantics allow your classes to transfer ownership of internal resources—pointers, buffers, handles—without making costly deep copies. When such objects are returned from factories or inserted into vectors, moves eliminate deep copy loops.
